Subject: Sizing ask: steady run-rate + surge strategy for private GPU pool

Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're moving toward a private deployment (VPC) with Redwood and need help turning our traffic profile into a concrete GPU sizing and network/egress plan. High level:

- Steady-state: ~1.2k inference requests per minute (mixed chat + short generations), roughly 14k tokens/minute aggregate.
- Peak windows: up to 6x steady for 3-12 minute bursts, 4-6 times per day.
- Tail-latency SLO: 99th < 350ms internal goal (customer-facing will be conservative).
- Data egress cap: our network team has set a hard egress budget of 6 TB/day from the VPC.

Can you propose: a steady-state GPU pool sizing, a warm-pool/burst amortization approach, and recommendations for staying within the egress cap while honoring SLOs? We'd like concrete assumptions (GPU type, estimated QPS per card, KV cache warmup amortization, admissions policy).

We can do a 30-minute call this week if that helps.

Regards,
Arielle Chen
Director, Platform Ops — Helios Labs

Arielle —

Thanks, this is exactly the right level of detail. I've sketched a first-pass run-rate model and a short playbook attached (runrate_model_marissa_v2.xlsx). Key assumptions up front so we're explicit:

- Model family: 13B-30B class with dynamic KV caching; we sized per-req token average = 11 tokens; generation tail average = 48 tokens.
- GPU target: NVIDIA A100-80GB (on-prem rack equivalence). We assume ~1400 steady RPS per 8-card pod when KV warmed and batching is enabled (see tab "batching_assumptions").
- Warm-pool strategy: maintain 10% of steady pool as fully warmed (prefill KV, keep model partitions hot). Surges handled by a graduated warm-up (Sustained-Surge Amortization Window, SSAW) that pauses non-critical cache evictions for 8 minutes after a burst starts.
- Egress arithmetic: we model 6 TB/day as a hard cap. With our steady assumptions that maps to ~3.2k tokens/sec allowable egress; during bursts we suggest graceful degradation (quality knob + reduced response length) to keep within the cap.

Proposed immediate plan (short):
1) Run the attached model with your real traffic sample — we can update assumptions in the sheet.
2) Book a 30-minute alignment to confirm burst frequency and acceptable quality degradation thresholds.
3) If accepted, we convert the runbook into a committed-pool proposal + per-day egress guardrails and a canary schedule.

I've scheduled a 30-min slot tomorrow afternoon on the calendar tentatively.

Marissa / Jonas —

Reading Arielle's numbers. Quick internal notes and numbers to validate before the call:

- Baseline throughput assumption (warmed, batching 16 tokens/req avg): we should assume 8x A100-80GB pods deliver ~1.4k RPS per pod for chat-dominant workloads; that aligns with Marissa's sheet but call it out.
- Admission control: set soft admission at 1.2x steady (buffer) and hard cap at 2.5x steady per pod. Beyond hard cap, route to degraded profile (truncate length + prefer cached completions).
- Warm-pool sizing: 10% of pods fully warmed reduces first-token latency by ~35% for the first 90s of a burst. For Helios' 3-12 minute bursts, SSAW = 8 minutes gives best amortization for cache hit recovery without overspending on warm pool.
- Egress strategy (egress arbitration): two levers — (A) payload compression + protocol-level dedupe (we can save ~12% on egress), (B) adaptive length control: throttle generation length as a function of daily spend remaining. Propose egress throttle policy: if day-to-date egress >= 85% of budget, engage aggressive length cap and route non-critical requests to best-effort model variants.
- GPU count proposal (initial commit): steady-state requirement -> 3 pods (24 A100s) for headroom & canary margin; burst absorption (6x) met by warm-pool + admission policies, not by entire scale-to capacity — avoids overprovisioning and keeps cost predictable. We'll show alternatives in the sheet: conservative (40 cards), aggressive (18 cards).

I added a new tab to Marissa's sheet with these three sizing buckets and the egress-tracking heuristics.

Karthik
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
